title: Thai ghosts / ผีไทย: set the scare level by age before picking a spirit
text: The same Thai spirit can be cute or terrifying, so pick the tone from the players first. Kids 6-9: round, big-eyed, glowing friends who are lost or hungry and need help home, morning or evening light, no gore, no faces close to the camera. Teens 13-17: eerie but not gory, spooky or night lighting, slow reveals at the side of the route, never a jump scare that makes a walking player run. Adults: folklore atmosphere and story, still no blood or organs, because the scenery is low-poly and gore reads as cheap rather than scary.
use_when: any brief that mentions Thai ghosts, ผี, haunted or spooky with Thai culture
do: Ask or infer the youngest player before choosing a spirit
Kids: frame every ghost as someone to help
Teens: let ghosts stand beside the route and turn as you pass
Keep ghosts 1.5 m or more from the walking line in MR
avoid: Gore, entrails or blood at any age
Sudden scares that make a headset player run
Using the scariest spirit as the first thing kids see
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Mae Nak / แม่นาค: the loyal ghost wife, a love story first
text: Mae Nak of Phra Khanong is a tale of a wife who waits for her husband even after death, so the strongest hook is love and loyalty, not horror. The catalog has her stilt house, canal banks, rowboats, a swinging cradle, a lullaby note marker and the famous long arm reaching for a dropped lime. For kids, the route can be "Help Mae Nak find the limes before dawn" with a lullaby at each checkpoint; for teens, the long arm reaching across the canal makes a great side spectacle beside a hazard. End at dawn with the portal so the story closes gently.
use_when: a Thai ghost runner or story where a famous named folk spirit is wanted
do: Use canal, stilt house and cradle vignettes along a riverside route
Checkpoint labels that follow the story (cradle, lime tree, canal, dawn)
Lighting evening for kids, spooky for teens
avoid: Recreating the look or scenes of a specific Mae Nak film or series
Referencing her real shrine or turning worship into score
Making her a boss that is beaten up

title: Krasue / กระสือ: the floating glowing head, toned without gore
text: The krasue is a floating woman's head trailing glowing organs, which is too graphic as told. In low-poly, show only the head and a soft glowing ribbon trail (the catalog has green-glow, pink-coil and flying-trail versions plus a Krasue Queen boss). For kids it is a shy night-light spirit that drifts over the rice fields; for teens its trail can mark where a hazard is, and the Krasue Queen works as a battle boss name in a dark theme. Keep the trail abstract light, never organs.
use_when: a brief wants a famous scary Thai ghost, a night-time glow or a battle boss with Thai flavour
do: Describe the trail as a glowing ribbon in prompts
Use night or spooky lighting so the glow reads
Pair with rice fields, banana groves and village huts
avoid: Drawing entrails, blood or a severed neck
Krasue in daylight outdoors where the glow vanishes
Putting the floating head at eye level right on the route

title: Phi Pop / ผีปอบ: never design a "find the possessed villager" game
text: In folklore the phi pop possesses a person and eats their insides, and real villagers, often older women, have been accused of being phi pop and driven out of their homes. So a game where players accuse or hunt a villager hidden in a crowd repeats a real harm. Use the catalog's old-woman and old-man phi pop as clearly supernatural, comic-grumpy spirits who steal snacks from the kitchen, and make the player return the snacks, not punish anyone.
use_when: a brief mentions ผีปอบ, possession or a hidden-monster-among-villagers idea
do: Make phi pop obviously a ghost (glow, float), never an ordinary villager
Kids: snack-stealing grump, players carry snacks home along the route
Keep eating and organ details off screen
avoid: Accusation or witch-hunt mechanics
Elderly women as the default monster look
Gore about eaten organs

title: Nang Tani / นางตานี: the banana-tree lady as a gentle guide
text: Nang Tani lives in wild banana trees and is usually told as a beautiful, mostly harmless spirit in green, which makes her one of the best Thai ghosts for children and families. The catalog has the Tani banana-tree lady plus young, fruiting and tattered banana clumps, a firefly tree and glow mushrooms. Build a banana grove route where she points the way: each checkpoint is a banana clump with a soft glow, and the portal is a moonlit clearing. Evening lighting keeps faces friendly; night makes the green glow pop indoors.
use_when: a family or kids brief that wants Thai folklore without fear
do: Banana grove vignettes 1.5 m beside the route
Labels like "Follow the green light"
Use her as the guide on the intro card
avoid: Turning her into a seductive figure for kids
Cutting down banana trees as a goal
Spooky lighting for under-8s

title: Phi Am / ผีอำ: the sleep-pressure ghost needs care with bedrooms
text: Phi Am is the spirit that sits on a sleeper's chest, the folk name for sleep paralysis, which is a real frightening experience for many people. For teens and adults, a haunted-house interior (the catalog has teak beds with mosquito nets, wardrobes ajar, rocking chairs, dust-sheet sofas and the Phi Am shadow sitter) makes a strong spooky runner indoors at night. For kids, skip the bedroom setting and show Phi Am as a sleepy heavy shadow who just wants a pillow, placed in a garden, not over a bed.
use_when: a haunted house, bedroom or sleep-themed ghost idea
do: Teens: interior route room by room with spooky lighting
Keep the shadow sitter as scenery, not jumping out
Kids: move it outdoors and make it sleepy and comic
avoid: A bed scene where the player lies down or is pinned
Bedroom horror for under-10s
Text that describes real sleep paralysis symptoms

title: Pret / เปรต: the tall hungry ghost works as a "feed them" goal
text: Pret are very tall hungry ghosts with tiny mouths from Buddhist teaching about greed, and Thai children know them from temple murals. The playful, respectful angle is generosity: the catalog has tall and hunched pret, a Pret King boss, a pret-mouth target hoop and trays of throw food (rice balls, khanom krok, sticky rice). A runner where each checkpoint "feeds" a pret turns them from scary to sad-and-helped. In battle, Pret King can be a dark-theme boss name, but the line should be "send them to rest", not mockery of the teaching.
use_when: a ghost theme for kids or a battle boss with a Thai folk name
do: Checkpoints as feeding stops with food props in vignettes
Keep the pret 2 m or more from the line, they are 3 m tall
Frame the end as the ghosts finally full and at peace
avoid: Recreating temple murals of the hell realms
Food thrown at elders or monks
Gags about the teaching itself

title: Phi Ta Khon / ผีตาโขน: a joyful ghost parade, not a horror theme
text: Phi Ta Khon is a festival in Dan Sai, Loei (usually around June or July), where people wear bright masks made from rice-steaming baskets and coconut-tree bases and dance through town. It is colourful, noisy and merry, so treat it as a parade theme: the catalog has a Phi Ta Khon festival mask figure and a mask jack-o-lantern. A runner that follows a parade street with banners and dancing mask figures beside the route suits families at noon or evening light, since the colours survive daylight.
use_when: a festival, parade or Isan theme, or "Thai ghosts but fun"
do: Treat masks as festival art: bright, many colours, lined along the route
Label checkpoints as parade stops
Use noon or evening; the theme survives outdoor light
avoid: Spooky lighting and horror framing
Inventing fake ritual meanings for the masks
Calling it Halloween

title: Phi Khamot / ผีโขมด: will-o-wisps as the kindest guide lights
text: Khamot are floating lights in the dark fields that lead travellers astray in folklore. Flip it into a guide: the catalog has orb, flame and trio wisps plus firefly clusters and fog bands. A wisp hovering above each checkpoint gives first-time VR kids a target they can see from far away without reading text. The light reads only in night or spooky lighting indoors, or evening at a dim venue.
use_when: a night route for young or first-time players who need visual wayfinding
do: Put a wisp above each checkpoint at 1.6-2 m height
Use fog bands only beside the route, not hiding hazards
Story line: "the lights lead you home"
avoid: Wisps that lead into hazards as a trick for kids
Glow themes outdoors at noon
More than one wisp colour meaning different things

title: In battle, Thai spirits are sent to rest, not killed
text: Thai ghost stories usually end with a spirit being calmed, given merit or let go, so slashing ghosts to death feels off to many Thai players and parents. Keep the battle engine as it is (grunts, shields, beasts, a boss) but write the chapter lines and boss intro as releasing restless spirits before dawn: "Calm the wandering spirits", "Free the Pret King". The verbs change the meaning with no change to mechanics.
use_when: a battle game with Thai ghosts as enemies
do: Use dark or forest theme with lines about calming or freeing
Final chapter: dawn, the boss is set free
Boss names from folklore types, or invented
avoid: Chapter lines like "Kill the ghosts"
Monks, temple objects or sacred amulets as weapons in the story
Gloating victory text over a spirit

title: Himmapan forest / ป่าหิมพานต์: a golden mythic sky world
text: The Himmapan is the mythical forest of Thai art, full of hybrid creatures, which gives a fantasy world that is clearly Thai without touching anything sacred. The catalog has a full set: golden gates and sky portals, floating islands with golden salas and spires, lotus platforms, naga bridges, kinnaree, golden swans, white elephants and golden-leaf trees. It suits a runner as a "journey through the sky forest" or a void-floor dramatic finale, and the gold reads in daylight, so noon and morning work outdoors.
use_when: a fantasy theme that should feel Thai, elegant, or for tourists
do: Name the realm and its creatures in the story
Use golden gate arches as checkpoint frames
Morning or evening light for warm gold
avoid: Putting Buddha images or temple chedis on the islands
Mixing in royal regalia as treasure
Too many gold props so hazards stop standing out

title: Naga / พญานาค: a revered guardian, use as rails and allies, not a slain boss
text: Naga serpents guard temple stairs and rivers and are honoured as protectors, especially in the Mekong region and Isan, where many people believe in them sincerely. Use naga as bridge railings, stair rails and gates (the catalog has naga-railed bridges, naga-head newels and a sweeping naga tail) and as a friendly guide in the story. If a battle needs a water serpent foe, invent a different creature (a "river wyrm" or "mud eel") with its own look rather than defeating a naga.
use_when: a water, river or Himmapan theme, or a serpent enemy is wanted
do: Naga railing along a bridge section of the route
Story: the naga guards the river and lets you cross
Invent a non-naga serpent for any enemy role
avoid: A naga as the defeated boss
Stepping on naga heads as hazards
Joke or cute-dumb naga for adults in Isan

title: Garuda / ครุฑ: a Himmapan bird is fine, the state emblem pose is not
text: The garuda is a great half-bird hero of Himmapan art, but in Thailand a red and gold garuda with spread wings and raised arms is the royal and state emblem, seen on official buildings and documents. A game must not use that emblem look on badges, banners, prizes or as an enemy. If a creator wants a garuda, show it as a flying creature in the sky or perched far away, in a different pose and colour scheme, and never on a crest.
use_when: a brief asks for garuda, a bird hero or a "Thai kingdom" crest
do: Garuda flying in the background sky or on a distant island
Invent the kingdom crest (a lotus, a star lantern)
Choose a different colour mix from red and gold
avoid: The spread-wing red-gold emblem pose anywhere
Garuda as an enemy or captured target
Garuda logo on the game title

title: Kinnaree / กินรี: graceful bird-maidens for gates and dance moments
text: Kinnaree are half-woman half-swan dancers of grace and beauty, known from Thai classical dance. The catalog has flying kinnaree, a circling pair, a kinnaree wing gate and a bird-maiden dancer. Use them as the gatekeepers of checkpoints (wings open as you approach) and as the sensation moment for spectators. Keep the costume graceful and covered, a cultural art form, and avoid sexualised poses.
use_when: a Himmapan, dance, elegant or "beautiful Thai" theme
do: A kinnaree gate at the climax checkpoint facing spectators
Pair with lotus ponds and golden swans
Morning or evening light
avoid: Revealing or sexualised designs
Kinnaree as monsters or grunts
Using real dancers' photos as reference faces

title: Singha / สิงห์: guardian lions that frame the start and finish
text: Stone singha lions guard gateways in Thai and Lanna temples and palaces, which makes them natural markers for the start and the portal. The catalog has a stone singha guardian and a winged lion guardian statue. Place a pair either side of the spawn or the finish portal, facing outwards, 1.5 m clear of the walking line. On a tactics board story they can be the two "watchers" at the edge of a courtyard, but never pieces to capture.
use_when: framing the entrance or finish of a Thai or Lanna themed game
do: Pairs, symmetric, at spawn or portal
Use as scenery outside the board in tactics
Combine with lanterns and tung banners
avoid: Singha as enemies or hazards
Placing them on the route where players brush past
Using a real brand's lion logo

title: Songkran / สงกรานต์: Thai New Year water festival, 13-15 April
text: Songkran is the Thai New Year, 13 to 15 April, the hottest time of year, known for water fights in the streets (Chiang Mai's moat is famous) and the gentle custom of pouring scented water over elders' hands for blessing. In a runner, checkpoints can be "Splash station" stops along a street with water jars, buckets, flower garlands and a moat bank, hazards as slippery puddles. Show the elder blessing as a calm vignette, not a joke. Noon and morning lighting fit the bright, sunny mood.
use_when: a festival theme in March or April, a water theme, or a Thai New Year event
do: Street route with water jar and garland vignettes
Hazards as puddles or slippery tiles
A calm blessing vignette near the end
avoid: Splashing monks or elders as gags
Spooky or night lighting
Promising water-gun shooting (the engine cannot shoot)

title: Songkran in MR: the water must stay virtual
text: Creators planning a Songkran booth sometimes want real water play next to the game. Quest 3 headsets and controllers are not waterproof, and wet floors make walking players slip. Keep all water in the virtual scene, place the booth away from street water fights, and use a covered, dry floor; suggest spectators throw cheers, not water.
use_when: an MR booth during Songkran or a water-play request
do: Ask where the booth is relative to water play
Dry, covered floor and a towel station
Virtual splash moments at checkpoints
avoid: Real water guns near players
Outdoor booth on a wet street
Water props on the real floor
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Loy Krathong / ลอยกระทง: float a light on the river
text: Loy Krathong falls on the full moon of the 12th Thai lunar month, usually in November, when people float krathong (banana-trunk rafts with flowers, a candle and incense) on rivers to thank the water and let go of bad luck. It is calm and pretty, so the runner fits submission and narrative: walk a riverside route, each checkpoint lights a lantern, and the portal is the water's edge where you "float your wish". Night lighting indoors makes candles glow; the catalog has lotus lanterns, lily pads, piers and a krathong lantern.
use_when: a festival theme in November, a calm couples or family experience, or a river theme
do: Riverside or canal route, portal at the water edge
Labels as wishes or thanks
Night lighting indoors, evening outdoors
avoid: Fast race or harsh hazards that break the calm
Foam krathong props (the culture now prefers natural ones)
Mixing in Halloween wording in November

title: Yi Peng / ยี่เป็ง: Lanna lantern night in Chiang Mai
text: Yi Peng is the Lanna festival held at the same full moon as Loy Krathong, famous in Chiang Mai for hanging lanterns (khom fai), star lanterns and sky lanterns (khom loi). A lantern trail runner is the natural fit: the route winds under Lanna hexagon and star lanterns, each checkpoint lights one, and the finale releases a sky lantern above the portal for spectators to see. Sky lanterns are now restricted for fire safety, so show them as a virtual-only moment and never suggest releasing real ones at the venue.
use_when: a Chiang Mai, Lanna or lantern brief, especially October to November
do: Lanterns hung above or beside the route, never at head height on it
One rising virtual lantern as the climax
Night or evening lighting
avoid: Real sky lantern release or open flames
Temple ordination areas as the setting
Too many lights so hazards disappear

title: Chiang Mai Flower Festival: floats and gardens, early February
text: The Chiang Mai Flower Festival takes place on the first weekend of February with a parade of flower-covered floats and big flower displays in the park, during the cool, dry season. It makes a bright daytime theme: a garden route with giant flowers, a float parade of animal shapes, bougainvillea and marigold bushes. The catalog's garden set (giant daisy and flower-head platforms, petal pennants, bluebell lamps) works with Lanna lanterns on top. Noon or morning lighting is ideal and survives outdoors.
use_when: a spring, garden or Chiang Mai daytime event, January to February
do: Float-shaped vignettes beside a parade route
Petal-pennant flags as checkpoints
Gentle, family pacing with few hazards
avoid: Night lighting that hides the colours
Copying a real company's sponsored float logo
Pollen and bee hazards for very young kids without care

title: Vegetarian Festival / เทศกาลกินเจ: use the food and flags, not the piercing rites
text: The Vegetarian (Jay) Festival runs nine days in the ninth Chinese lunar month (September to October), famous in Phuket and Bangkok's Chinatown, with yellow flags marked with the red character for jay, white clothing, vegetarian food stalls and firecrackers. Some processions include self-piercing by spirit mediums, which is sacred to devotees and too graphic for a game. Use the yellow-flag street food market as the theme: stalls, lanterns and a parade street, with no piercing, blood or trance figures.
use_when: a brief mentions กินเจ, Jay, Phuket festival or a yellow-flag food market
do: Yellow flags and food stalls along a street route
Checkpoints as stalls to visit
Evening lighting for lanterns
avoid: Pierced faces, blades or fire-walking scenes
Making spirit mediums into monsters
Meat props in a vegetarian festival scene

title: Bun Bang Fai / บุญบั้งไฟ: Isan rocket festival, May
text: Bun Bang Fai is held in Isan (Yasothon is the best known) in May, before the rains, when villages build and launch home-made bamboo rockets to call the rain. It suits a high-energy theme: a runner through rice fields where each checkpoint "loads a rocket", and the finale launches one over the portal. The catalog has a bamboo rocket (bang fai) launcher, buffalo carts, rice granaries and sugar palms. Some parades include rude jokes and phallic props, so leave those out for family games.
use_when: an Isan theme, a festival in April to May, or a launch-and-celebrate climax
do: Rice-field route with rocket launcher vignette at the end
Noon or evening lighting
Spectator moment: the virtual launch
avoid: Phallic or rude parade props
Players near real fireworks
Rockets as projectiles players fire (no shooting)

title: Chinese New Year in Thailand / ตรุษจีน: red lanterns and lion dance streets
text: Chinese New Year (January or February) is big in Bangkok's Yaowarat, in Phuket and in many Thai-Chinese homes: red lanterns, gold, red envelopes, oranges, lion and dragon dances and firecrackers. A runner down a lantern-lit market street (round Chinese paper lanterns, shophouses, fruit stalls) with the dragon or lion dancers beside the route makes a cheerful family theme. Keep ancestor altars and shrines as quiet background, not interactive props.
use_when: a January to February event, a Thai-Chinese community, or a red-and-gold festive theme
do: Red lantern strings above the route edge
Checkpoints as "collect luck" stops (oranges, red envelopes)
Evening or night lighting
avoid: Ancestor altars or joss offerings as hazards
Accents or costumes that mock Chinese people
Real firecrackers near the play area

title: After a festival date, rename the theme instead of dropping it
text: A festival theme feels stale or wrong the day after the event, but the art is still useful. Rename it: Songkran becomes a "water splash festival", Loy Krathong and Yi Peng become a "lantern river night", Christmas becomes a "winter village" after 26 December, Halloween becomes a "ghost night" or "spirit festival" after 31 October. Keep the props, change the title, story and labels, and remove the dated wording from the intro card.
use_when: a brief or event that runs past a festival's date, or a long-running booth
do: Check the event dates against the festival date
Swap dated words in title, story, labels
Keep the scenery and palette
avoid: Festival names in titles after the day
Countdown or "tonight" wording for a multi-week event
Rebuilding the whole scene just to rename it

title: Thai night market / ตลาดกลางคืน: stalls, lights and a winding walk
text: A Thai night market is rows of stalls under string lights, with food smoke, music and crowds, which maps neatly onto a runner: the route winds between stall vignettes and each checkpoint is a stall to visit ("Buy the meatball skewer", "Find the lantern seller"). The catalog has market stalls, sweets stalls, cloth stalls, fruit stalls with parasols, lantern posts and paper lantern strings. Night or evening lighting gives the right glow; hazards can be spilled ice or a puddle.
use_when: a market, food, tourist or Chiang Mai evening theme
do: Stalls as vignettes 1 m or more beside the route
Labels as shopping errands
Night lighting indoors, evening outdoors
avoid: Stalls on the route that players walk into
Real shop or brand names on signs
Crowded corners where two lanes cross

title: Floating market / ตลาดน้ำ: boats, canals and fruit
text: Floating markets sell fruit, noodles and flowers from small wooden boats on canals, a classic central-Thailand image. The catalog's lotus city set has bobbing longtail fruit boats, flower boats, a sampan with a frog vendor, piers with pavilions, canal banks and mooring poles. Lay the route along the canal bank with boats drifting beside it; the canal itself can be a void-floor drop in VR, or simply water scenery in MR with a plank bridge to cross. Morning lighting fits, since markets open at dawn.
use_when: a water, canal, food or central Thai theme
do: Route along the bank with one bridge crossing
Boats as moving scenery beside the path
Morning light, colourful fruit
avoid: Asking players to "step into a boat" in MR
Hazards placed on the bridge itself
Overdressing so the canal is not readable

title: Rice fields / ทุ่งนา: open green paddies with village life
text: Rice paddies are the heart of rural Thailand: flat green squares, raised earth paths between them, a wooden hut, buffalo, scarecrows and a rice granary. The raised paths form a natural grid, which fits a tactics board story ("cross the paddies without waking the scarecrows") as well as a calm runner. The catalog has rice granaries, buffalo carts, haystacks, scarecrows with ngob hats, sticky-rice baskets and banana trees. Morning or noon light suits daytime farm life; at night it becomes the stage for krasue and khamot stories.
use_when: a countryside, farm, Isan or calm daylight theme
do: Tactics: describe the board as paddies and earth paths
Runner: zig-zag along paddy edges
Buffalo and huts as vignettes
avoid: Showing poverty as a joke
Buffalo as enemies
Too uniform, add huts and trees for landmarks

title: Doi Suthep mountain feel: mist and forest, not the temple
text: Creators in Chiang Mai often want "Doi Suthep", the mountain west of the city. Its sacred temple, golden chedi and naga staircase are a pilgrimage site, so do not recreate them as a game level. Capture the mountain feel instead: misty forest, mossy boulders, winding stone steps, viewpoint over a city of lights, cool morning air. Use fog wisps beside the route, old conifers and stepping stones, and a viewpoint portal at the top facing spectators.
use_when: a brief asks for Doi Suthep, a mountain, a Chiang Mai landmark or a misty forest
do: Mountain path route that climbs in a spiral
Morning lighting with fog wisps
A viewpoint finale over a distant city
avoid: Recreating the real chedi or temple stairs
Climbing real stairs in MR
Monks on the route as scenery

title: Old city moat and walls / คูเมือง: a square city with corner bastions
text: Chiang Mai's old city is a square ringed by a moat and old brick walls with gates and corner bastions, and many Thai towns have similar old walls. This shape makes a loop route around a walled square, with each gate as a checkpoint and the corner bastions as landmarks. The catalog has brick city walls, bastions with banners, a city gate, laterite plaza tiles and lamp posts. Invent the city's name (as in "Phayakburi") rather than copying a real gate's sign.
use_when: a Chiang Mai, old town or "kingdom" theme, or a loop route
do: Four gates as four checkpoints on a loop
Moat as water scenery outside the route
Evening lighting, lanterns on walls
avoid: Real gate names on signs
Walls placed where they hide spectators' view
Royal crests on banners

see_also.why: Lynch's image of the city (paths, edges, nodes, landmarks) directly matches using the moat as an edge, gates as nodes/checkpoints and bastions as landmarks on a loop route.

title: Lanna style / ล้านนา: northern Thai teak, kalae and star lanterns
text: Lanna is the old northern kingdom centred on Chiang Mai, with its own look: dark teak houses on stilts, crossed kalae boards on the gable tips, tung banners (long hanging flags), hexagon and star paper lanterns, woven bamboo, sticky-rice baskets and red, gold and deep green accents. In low-poly, lean on silhouettes: steep stacked roofs, long tung banners, a lantern line. It is warm and welcoming, and tourists recognise it, so it fits both a family runner and an elegant tactics courtyard.
use_when: a northern Thai, Chiang Mai or "Thai but not Bangkok" visual direction
do: Name the style "Lanna-inspired" in prompts
Tung banners as checkpoint flags
Star lanterns hung at the route edge
avoid: Mixing in central Thai palace roofs and calling it Lanna
Temple ordination halls as the main building
Hill-community costumes as decoration

title: Temples: distant backdrop only, never part of the action
text: Temple scenery (chedis, halls, bell towers) can set the mood of a Thai world, but it must stay respectful. Keep any temple model at the far edge of the scene as backdrop, not on the route, not inside a battle arena, not as a tactics target or board feature, and never a hazard. Prefer ruined, generic or invented structures (a ruined bell chedi in an ancient forest) over anything that looks like a real active temple, and never build an interior with altars.
use_when: any Thai theme where temple models are tempting
do: Place temple models 3 m or more outside the route
Prefer invented ruins and pavilions
Use them for skyline, not interaction
avoid: Battle enemies spawning from a temple
Checkpoints on temple steps
Temple interiors, altars or Buddha images

title: Spirit houses and offerings: scenery to respect, never hazards
text: Most Thai homes and shops have a spirit house (san phra phum) with daily offerings, and many players treat them seriously. The catalog has spirit houses, garlands, bai si towers, incense, fruit platters and even pig-head offerings. Place them as quiet vignettes beside the route, perhaps marking the start as "the guardian of this land", but never as hazards, things to kick, targets to capture, or score pickups.
use_when: a Thai village, house or ghost theme that uses offering props
do: A spirit house vignette near the spawn as a welcome
Keep offerings upright, tidy and clear of the route
Story: the guardian spirit blesses the journey
avoid: Knocking over or stepping on offerings
Offering food as collectible points
Pig heads in kids' scenes

title: Yantra, amulets and takrut: keep them invented and off the floor
text: Yantra cloths, takrut scrolls and amulets are sacred to many Thai people, who wear and bless them. The catalog includes floating yantra and takrut pickups, which are acceptable when the patterns are clearly invented fantasy runes and they float at checkpoints. Do not place them on the floor to be stepped on, do not copy a real monastery's yantra design, and do not make amulets a gacha or loot reward.
use_when: a design that uses yantra, amulet or talisman props
do: Floating at checkpoint height (1.2-1.6 m)
Invented patterns in prompts ("fantasy rune cloth")
A few as story items, not dozens
avoid: Floor hazards shaped as yantra
Copies of real sak yant designs
Amulets as random loot

title: Thai street food stall: an errand route kids and tourists love
text: Thai street food is a shared pride and an easy hook for any visitor: noodle carts, grilled meatball skewers, khanom krok in a dimpled pan, sticky rice in a woven basket, iced drinks in plastic bags. A runner where each checkpoint is "the next order" gives a clear goal and a fun finish ("Serve the hungry ghost" or "Bring dinner home"). The catalog has charcoal stoves, woks, skewers, khanom krok, sticky rice balls and coconut carts.
use_when: a food theme, a tourist booth, or kids who need a simple goal
do: Checkpoint labels as orders ("Grab the khanom krok")
Stall vignettes with stove and parasol
Evening lighting for cooking smoke and lamps
avoid: Real restaurant or vendor names
Jokes about tourists being sick from food
Hazards shaped as food

title: Mango sticky rice / ข้าวเหนียวมะม่วง: a gather-the-ingredients runner
text: Mango sticky rice is sweet sticky rice with coconut milk and ripe mango, a favourite in the hot season (March to May). It gives a neat story loop for kids: four checkpoints gather the parts in order (mango tree, sticky-rice basket, coconut cart, the plate), the portal is the shared dessert table. The catalog has mango trees with fruit, sticky-rice baskets, young coconuts and toke dining trays. Noon or morning light keeps the yellow and white bright.
use_when: a short kids or family runner with a food goal
do: Order the checkpoints like a recipe
Keep 4-5 checkpoints for under-8s
Finish at a table vignette spectators can see
avoid: Long text describing the recipe
Rotten or gross food gags
Dark lighting

title: Muay Thai / มวยไทย: theme the world, the engine still swings a sword
text: Muay Thai is a national pride and a natural "battle" request, but the battle engine is a sword (PC: 3-hit combo and dash; MR: the right controller is the sword), with no punches, kicks or clinch. Offer a Muay Thai camp as the world and story (ring ropes, sandbags, tyres, training camp boards) with the sword battle, or a training-camp runner where checkpoints are drills. Treat the wai khru dance and the mongkhon headband as respected traditions shown in the intro, never as hazards or loot.
use_when: a brief asks for Muay Thai, boxing, kicking or punching
do: Say kindly that the engine swings a sword, not fists
Offer krabi krabong (Thai sword art) as the honest fit
Runner alternative: a training-camp route
avoid: Promising punch or kick detection
Mocking the wai khru
Stepping over or kicking a mongkhon prop

title: Krabi krabong / กระบี่กระบอง: the Thai sword art fits the battle engine
text: Krabi krabong is a traditional Thai martial art with swords, staffs and shields, shown at cultural festivals and in historical dramas. It matches the battle engine honestly: the player holds a sword, shields block from the front, and a beast charges. Write the chapters as a warrior training to defend a walled old town, use forest or desert theme for a sun-baked field, and give the boss an invented name, not a real historical king or hero.
use_when: a Thai warrior, historical or "Muay Thai but battle" brief
do: Story: train in a warrior camp, defend the town gate
Shield foes as the training partner chapter
Desert or forest theme
avoid: Real historical kings or national heroes as characters
Battles against neighbouring nations
Royal regalia as the boss reward

title: Elephants / ช้าง: free and gentle, no riding, no chains, no tricks
text: Elephants are the national animal of Thailand and beloved, and elephant tourism has moved away from riding, chains and circus tricks towards sanctuaries. Show elephants walking free in a forest, bathing in a river or as the gentle white elephant of Himmapan stories (the catalog has a white-elephant fountain, an island elephant and an elephant fruit merchant). Never put players on an elephant's back, never show hooks or chains, and never make an elephant a battle enemy or hazard.
use_when: any theme with elephants, jungle, Thailand tourism or Himmapan
do: Elephants as calm scenery beside the route
Story: help a lost baby elephant back to the herd
Spectator moment: elephant spray at the finish
avoid: Riding seats, chains, hooks or performances
Elephants as beasts in battle
Painted elephants for selfies

title: Isan (northeast Thailand) / อีสาน: rice, festivals and khaen music
text: Isan is the large northeastern region with strong Lao-Thai culture: rice fields and sugar palms, sticky rice in woven baskets, wooden stilt houses, buffalo, khaen pipe music, mor lam songs, the Bun Bang Fai rocket festival and Phi Ta Khon in Loei. It is warm, lively and proud. Show it as cheerful and resourceful, with the music and festivals as the energy, not as "poor countryside".
use_when: a brief mentions Isan, Lao-Thai culture, mor lam or the northeast
do: Rice-field and village vignettes, festival finale
Music stage props for a mor lam party
Noon or evening lighting
avoid: Poverty or accent jokes
Mixing Lanna lanterns in as "Isan"
Naga as an enemy (deeply believed in the Mekong region)

title: Southern Thailand / ภาคใต้: islands, longtail boats and old towns
text: The south is limestone islands, turquoise water, white beaches, longtail boats with ribbons on the bow, coconut palms, coral reefs and Phuket's Sino-Portuguese old town shophouses in pastel colours. It fits sunny noon runners (island hopping on plank bridges), an underwater reef world, or a pastel old-town street. The south is also home to Muslim communities, so mosques are backdrop with the same care as temples, and food scenes should not assume pork everywhere.
use_when: a beach, island, Phuket, reef or southern Thailand theme
do: Island-hopping route with plank and rope bridges
Pastel shophouses for an old-town street
Noon lighting outdoors
avoid: Religious buildings in the action area
Pork props in a scene meant for a Muslim community
Tsunami disaster as a theme

title: Central Thailand: river life, canals and ancient brick ruins
text: Central Thailand is the Chao Phraya river plain: stilt houses over canals, floating markets, rice, and the brick ruins of old capitals with tree roots and leaning chedis. Ruined brick and laterite walls, broken pavilions and a giant bodhi tree give an "ancient lost city" feeling that is Thai without being an active temple. Keep any Buddha head in tree roots out: it is a famous real image that is sacred, not decoration.
use_when: a canal, river, "ancient Thai city" or adventure-ruins brief
do: Ruined laterite walls and leaning chedis as distant scenery
Canal bank routes with plank bridges
Evening light on brick
avoid: The Buddha head in tree roots
Climbing ruins as checkpoints
Treasure-looting framing at real heritage sites

title: Hill communities: no costumes as decoration, no "exotic" spectacle
text: Northern Thailand is home to many highland peoples (Karen, Hmong, Akha, Lahu, Lisu and others) with their own languages, dress and beliefs. Do not use their clothing, faces or rituals as costumes, enemies, scenery "natives" or tourist spectacle, and never reference neck rings or other dress as a curiosity. If a creator wants a mountain-village feel, use terraced fields, mist, bamboo bridges and generic wooden houses; if a community wants its own story told, it should be designed with them.
use_when: a northern mountain, trekking or "hill tribe" theme request
do: Use landscape (terraces, mist, bamboo) for the mountain feel
Suggest working with the community for their own stories
Invented characters with no specific ethnic dress
avoid: "Hill tribe" costumes or masks as props
Neck-ring or traditional dress as a gag
Highland villagers as enemies or background extras

title: Buddha images: never props, targets, enemies or floor decor
text: Buddha images are deeply sacred in Thailand; even tattoos or decor showing the Buddha cause offence, and placing one low or near feet is disrespectful. In FortalLand a Buddha image must never appear as scenery, a checkpoint, a hazard, a tactics target, a boss or a collectible, in any genre. If a creator asks for one, explain kindly and offer a lotus, a golden bodhi tree, a lantern or an invented guardian spirit instead.
use_when: any brief that mentions Buddha, a temple game or a "holy statue"
do: Replace with lotus, bodhi tree or lantern symbols
Explain the reason in one friendly line
Check key art prompts do not include a seated Buddha
avoid: Buddha heads, statues or murals anywhere in the scene
"Collect the golden Buddhas"
Buddha images in key art backgrounds

title: Monks and novices: never enemies, jokes or hazards
text: Monks are highly respected in Thai society; women traditionally avoid touching them and people bow when meeting them. A monk or novice must not be an enemy, a comic character, a hazard, a chaser or a spectator gag. Most game stories need none; if a wise helper is wanted, use an invented hermit (ruesi-like but named and dressed as a fantasy sage), an old forest spirit or a talking animal instead.
use_when: a story needs a wise helper, or a brief mentions monks or temple life
do: Use a fantasy sage, owl elder or kind spirit as the guide
Keep saffron robes out of character designs
If monks appear in a real-event backdrop, keep them distant and calm
avoid: Monk enemies, zombie monks or ghost monks
Monks in silly poses or chasing players
Saffron robes on a villain

title: Royal symbols are off-limits: build an invented fantasy court
text: Royal portraits, crowns, regalia, the royal garuda, royal flags, royal barges and the names of real kings or queens are protected by Thai law and custom and must not appear as props, prizes, characters, enemies or jokes. A "kingdom", "palace" or "prince" story should use an invented realm with its own name, crest (a lotus, a star lantern, a white elephant) and fictional characters with no resemblance to real royals, and the palace architecture should be fantasy, not a copy of a real palace.
use_when: a brief mentions a king, palace, prince, princess or kingdom
do: Invent the realm name and a non-royal crest
Fantasy palace from Himmapan or sky-palace models
Characters as heroes, not monarchs
avoid: Crowns or regalia as a final treasure
Real palace look-alikes
Yellow royal-day colours with crests as a theme

title: Head high, feet low: place respected things above foot level
text: In Thai etiquette the head is the highest part of the body and the feet the lowest, so pointing feet at, or stepping over, respected things is rude. In MR the player's feet are the main interaction with the virtual floor: hazards and floor decals sit where people step. So never put faces of elders, spirit houses, lotus symbols, national flags or sacred patterns on floor tiles or hazards; place them as raised scenery beside the route and keep the floor to neutral ground, tiles and water.
use_when: designing floor decals, hazards or tactics squares in a Thai theme
do: Floor = ground, tiles, water, leaves
Respected symbols raised at 1 m or higher, beside the route
Hazards as puddles, cracks, thorns or fire
avoid: Flags or faces as floor tiles
Lotus or yantra decals that players step on
Spirit houses at floor level on the route

title: Castles and knights: a generic storybook kingdom
text: A castle is the easiest theme for UK players and kids everywhere: towers, keeps, gatehouses, banners and a drawbridge. The catalog has round and octagonal towers, a castle keep, gatehouse, wall bastions, a banner hall and a throne dais. It fits all three genres: a battle defending the castle gate (forest theme), a tactics board as the castle courtyard (knight piece first, naturally), or a runner from the gatehouse to the throne. Keep crests invented and avoid any famous film castle or royal family.
use_when: a medieval, knight, princess or UK heritage theme
do: Tactics: the knight piece in a courtyard story
Runner: gate, bridge, hall, tower, throne as checkpoints
Invented heraldry (a fox, a star)
avoid: A famous animated film castle silhouette
Real royal coats of arms
Crusades or religious war framing

title: Halloween: pumpkins, witches and friendly frights, late October
text: Halloween on 31 October is big in the UK and US and growing in Thailand: pumpkins, witches, black cats, bats, skeletons and trick-or-treat sweets. The catalog has a large party set (jack-o-lanterns, cauldrons, witch hats, bat bunting, candy bowls, sheet ghosts, cute skeletons) and a witch marsh world. For kids, keep it "spooky cute" in evening light; for teens and adults, spooky or night lighting indoors. Battle fits a dark theme with sheet-ghost chapters and a witch boss.
use_when: an event in October or a spooky-cute party theme
do: Use spooky-cute for families, dark-eerie for teens
Trick-or-treat checkpoints ("Fill the candy bag")
Indoor or after-dark venues for glow
avoid: Running it past 31 October with the Halloween name
Gore, real weapons or horror-film killers
Mixing Thai sacred items into the party props

title: Thai events: no Halloween wording from 1 November
text: For Fortal events in Thailand the team stops using the word Halloween (ฮาโลวีน) in titles, intro cards, labels and promo from 1 November, even when the event runs on into November. The ghost content itself can stay: rename it as a "ghost night", "spirit festival", "Thai ghost party" or a Loy Krathong lantern night, and replace jack-o-lantern wording with lanterns. Check the event dates first whenever a brief has a spooky or pumpkin theme.
use_when: a Thai event or booth that runs after 31 October with a spooky theme
do: Check the event dates in the interview
Rename to ghost night or spirit festival
Swap pumpkin wording for lanterns
avoid: "Halloween" in any title or label after 31 October
Countdown to Halloween text in November
Removing all ghosts when only the word must go

title: Christmas: a winter village with gifts, 1-26 December
text: Christmas fits December events in the UK and Thai malls alike: snowy pines, cabins, sleighs, gifts, lantern posts with wreaths and hot cocoa. The catalog's frost vale set has penguins, polar bears, a red sleigh, a frost elk, gift piles and glowing igloos. A runner "deliver the gifts before morning" with one gift stop per checkpoint is simple and cheerful. Keep it secular and generic: an invented gift-giver or animal helpers rather than a branded Santa design, and drop the name after 26 December.
use_when: an event in December or a winter gift theme
do: Gift delivery checkpoints in a village loop
Evening or night lighting for lights and glow
Penguin or elk helpers as guides
avoid: A drinks brand's Santa look
Nativity scenes as game props
Christmas wording in January

title: Bonfire Night (UK), 5 November: fireworks, not effigies
text: Bonfire Night (Guy Fawkes Night) on 5 November is a UK tradition of bonfires and fireworks in parks on cold, dark evenings. A runner across a dark field with a virtual bonfire glow and a fireworks finale over the portal fits families. The tradition includes burning a "guy" effigy, which is uncomfortable for kids and a burning human figure is not something to put in a game; show fireworks and toffee-apple stalls instead.
use_when: a UK event in early November or a fireworks theme
do: Night lighting, fireworks finale above the portal
Sparkler and toffee-apple stall vignettes
Keep the virtual bonfire 3 m or more from the route
avoid: Burning effigies

title: British seaside pier: boardwalk, carnival rides and gulls
text: The British seaside pier is a long boardwalk over the sea with arcades, carousels, candy floss and fish and chips. It is a perfect out-and-back or lanes runner: walk out along the pier with ride vignettes either side, and the portal at the end over the sea. The catalog's carnival set has bulb-lit boardwalks, carousels, popcorn stands, cotton-candy carts, ticket booths and ferris wheels. Noon lighting for a sunny day, evening for the bulb lights.
use_when: a UK seaside, summer or funfair theme
do: Out-and-back route along a boardwalk
Rides as moving scenery beside the lane
Gulls and bunting for landmarks
avoid: A real pier's name or arcade brand
Void-floor sea drop for first-time players
Gambling machines as props for kids

title: London-like city: generic big-city icons, invented names
text: A UK city theme reads quickly with a few generic icons: a clock tower, red buses, black cabs, terraced houses, a river with bridges, rain and umbrellas. Use a clock tower and a river bridge from the catalog and keep it "a London-like city" with an invented name, so it stays original and does not need landmark permissions. A rainy evening palette with street lamps suits a runner chase through streets, and the river bridge makes a great midpoint checkpoint.

do: Invent the city name and the street names
Clock tower and bridge as landmarks
Evening lighting with street lamps
avoid: Exact replicas of named landmarks as the main set

title: Ancient Egypt-inspired ruins: sand, sun and scarabs
text: Desert ruins with sandstone blocks, obelisks, scarabs and sun discs make a bright adventure theme that survives daylight outdoors. The catalog's desert set has rotating sundials, scarabs rolling sand balls, sandworms, sliding stone blocks, mosaic plazas and sun banners, and the battle engine has a desert theme with the brightest base light. Use invented gods and pharaohs; avoid mummies of real people or tomb-looting framing, and do not label mixed ancient styles as Egyptian.
use_when: a desert, pyramid, archaeology or adventure brief
do: Battle: desert theme, sand-beast as the beast
Runner: dig site to sun gate
Noon lighting outdoors
avoid: Real pharaoh names or real mummies

Treasure theft as the goal for a museum client

title: Jungle sun-temple ruins: invent the culture, do not blend real ones
text: The catalog's sun set (stepped pyramids, glyph steles, jaguar statues, macaw perches, cenote islands) is inspired by Mesoamerican ruins. Present it as an invented jungle civilisation with its own name, not as "Aztec" or "Maya", and do not mix it with Egyptian or Thai sacred art in one world. Avoid sacrifice imagery; the hook is lost jungle discovery, so discovery feelings and a winding runner fit best, with forest lighting and green glows.
use_when: a jungle ruins or "ancient civilisation" adventure brief
do: Name the invented civilisation in the story
Discovery runner with glyph steles as checkpoints
Pair with jungle and waterfall scenery
avoid: Human sacrifice scenes
Labelling real cultures inaccurately
Blending three ancient cultures into one

title: Norse-inspired: longhouses, frost and runes, invented
text: A Norse-inspired world uses fjords, snowy pines, longhouses, forges, dragon-headed ships and runes. The catalog's frost vale, forge and dragon sets cover it, and the battle engine's ice and lava themes suit a "frost giant" or "forge dragon" story. Use invented runes and invented gods or heroes; some real runes and symbols have been used by hate groups, so do not copy runic symbols or rune lines from real sources.
use_when: a viking, frost, dragon or forge adventure brief

Longship and forge vignettes
avoid: Real runes or symbols copied as decoration

title: Japanese-inspired: torii, sakura and dojo, generic and respectful
text: The catalog's ninja set has torii arches, pagoda islands, sakura trees, stone toro lanterns, koi ponds, red bridges, taiko pads and a moon-gate portal, which makes a calm or action theme. Torii and shrines are religious sites in Japan, so use torii as the gate of an invented world, not a real shrine, and never as a hazard. Avoid stereotyped accents, the rising-sun flag and recreating a famous ninja anime's headbands or villages.
use_when: a Japanese, ninja, sakura or dojo theme

Sakura and koi for a calm runner
Invent the village name
avoid: The rising-sun flag
A specific anime's symbols or characters
Shrine buildings as battle arenas

title: Dinosaurs and museums: discovery with a roar
text: Dinosaurs are loved by kids in every country and work for museums, schools and malls. The library has dinosaur island creatures and jungle scenery (tree ferns, ginkgo, monkey-puzzle trees, cliffs). A museum client usually wants learning: a runner where each checkpoint is a dinosaur with a one-line fact, finishing at a big skeleton or nest. In battle, a dinosaur can be the beast, but for young kids keep dinosaurs as giants to watch, not chasers.

title: Space: stations, planets and warp portals
text: Space reads instantly at any age and suits neon or night lighting indoors. The catalog's space set has neon gantries, glass tube bridges, docking plazas, ringed planets, hologram arrows, UFO beams and a neon warp portal. Runner: a mission across a station with system checks as checkpoints; battle: neon theme with robot grunts; void floor: a walk across space for confident teens. Invent agencies, ships and aliens, and avoid real space agency logos.

Planets as far backdrop
avoid: Famous film starships or helmets

title: Pirates: treasure islands and harbour towns, kid-friendly
text: Pirates suit kids and families: ships, docks, treasure chests, parrots, cannons and colonial harbour towns. The catalog has a deep pirate collection (ships, docks, fort walls, harbour towns by day and night, octopus tentacles, rocking decks). A treasure-map runner where each checkpoint is a map clue is a classic; tactics can be a ship deck board. Keep it comic adventure, invent the captain, and avoid famous film pirate looks.

title: Toy room: giant toys at shrink-ray scale
text: A toy world makes the player tiny among giant toys: spinning tops, jack-in-the-boxes, toy trains, dominoes, building-block bridges and a music-box carousel are all in the catalog. It is bright and safe for young kids and works in daylight. A tactics board as a giant chessboard on a bedroom floor is a natural fit. Keep toys generic: no famous brick, doll or figure brands.

title: Candy land: sweets, cakes and gummies
text: Candy worlds are joyful and readable for under-10s: lollipops, gummy bears, donuts, cakes, cookie stepping stones and candy-cane lamps are in the catalog. They fit birthday parties and family malls. Hazards can be sticky jam puddles; battle can be the neon or forest theme with gummy grunts. title: Ice and frost: crystal palaces and auroras
text: Ice worlds are calm, clean and cool: ice palaces, crystal spires, frozen ponds, aurora ribbons and snowy pines. The battle engine has an ice theme for a frost-beast story, and the frost vale set brings friendly animals. Ice is a great escape theme in hot Thai months (March to May) and a natural Christmas-to-February theme in the UK. Pale blues wash out at noon outdoors, so prefer indoor or evening.

title: Music world: piano bridges and drum stages
text: A music world turns instruments into the set: piano-key bridges, guitar fretboard decks, giant snare-drum plazas, metronome arms and golden-note save stands. It suits concerts, schools and festivals, and can carry Thai flavour by adding a khaen or ranat-shaped stage prop in the story. Neon lighting gives a concert feel indoors. title: Farm: barns, tractors and friendly animals
text: A farm is gentle and familiar in both the UK (barns, tractors, hay bales) and Thailand (rice, buffalo, chickens). The catalog's farm set has windmills, hay bales, scarecrows, tractors, sprinklers, pecking hens and patchwork-field platforms. A morning runner "wake up the farm" is great for kindergartens and seniors, with very soft hazards. Keep animals as friends, not enemies.

title: Jungle: vines, waterfalls and hidden ruins
text: The jungle works across cultures and covers both Thai forests and adventure stories: banyan trees, bamboo, ferns, vine curtains, river stones, rock arches and waterfalls. The battle engine has a forest theme (greens and warm torchlight) for a friendly adventure. Combine with gentle wildlife (birds, monkeys) and keep elephants as calm scenery. title: Underwater reef: coral, jellyfish and sunken ships

title: Thai festival calendar: which themes fit which month
text: January to February: Chinese New Year and the Chiang Mai Flower Festival (first weekend of February), in the cool season; March to May: hot season, Songkran (13-15 April), mango sticky rice and Bun Bang Fai rockets in May. June to July: Phi Ta Khon in Loei; September to October: Vegetarian Festival, rainy season (go indoors) and Halloween up to 31 October. November: Loy Krathong and Yi Peng at the full moon of the 12th lunar month, with no Halloween wording; December: Christmas in malls and the New Year countdown. Lunar festivals move every year, so check the exact dates.

Check lunar festival dates for the year
Rename themes after their date
avoid: Songkran theme in December
Halloween wording in November
Assuming lunar festivals fall on the same day every year

title: UK calendar and daylight: which themes fit which month
text: UK seasons shape both theme and light. Winter (December to February) gets dark around 16:00, so night themes work even outdoors in late afternoon; Christmas fits 1-26 December. Spring (March to May) suits gardens and Easter-style egg hunts (keep it secular). Summer (June to August) stays light until about 21:00, so dark themes outdoors fail; seaside and festivals fit. Autumn: harvest, Halloween (31 October) and Bonfire Night (5 November).
use_when: a UK event, or a creator who lists a month and an outdoor venue

avoid: Night themes outdoors on a June evening

Halloween branding after 31 October for Thai teams

title: Thai seasons decide indoor or outdoor play
text: Thailand has a hot season (March to May, often above 35 C), a rainy season (June to October, sudden heavy storms) and a cool, dry season (November to February), the best time for outdoor events. In the north, February to April also brings smoke haze from field burning, so outdoor play in Chiang Mai can be unhealthy then. Headsets overheat in direct sun. Use outdoor themes from November to February and plan indoor venues for the rest.
use_when: an outdoor Thai venue or a creator who mentions a month

Shade, water and short sessions in hot months
avoid: Midday outdoor sessions in April
Outdoor plans in Chiang Mai haze season without a backup
Rainy-season events with no cover

title: Themes that make good battle enemies
text: The battle engine needs foes the player is happy to hit: robots (neon), lava or forge creatures (lava), frost beasts (ice), restless spirits sent to rest (dark), mummies or sand beasts (desert), goblin-like forest critters (forest). Map grunts to small foes, shields to armoured foes and the beast to the big one: robot drones, shield bots and a mech; imps, armoured golems and a lava beast. Avoid real animals people love, real peoples, monks or sacred beings as enemies.
use_when: choosing the theme and boss of a battle option
do: Pick one of the six engine themes, then write story to match
Match grunt/shield/beast to small/armoured/big
Invent boss names
avoid: Elephants, naga or monks as foes
Real nationalities or ethnic groups as enemies
Human soldiers for young kids

title: Themes that suit a tactics board
text: A 6 x 8 tactics board needs a setting where a grid feels natural: a castle courtyard with stone tiles, a marble palace plaza, a rice-paddy field of earth paths, a market of stall rows, a floating market canal grid, a toy-room floor, a ship deck. Guards become castle sentries, scarecrows, market watchmen or toy soldiers; tables become stalls or haystacks. Keep sacred places off the board: a Lanna-style pavilion courtyard is fine, a temple courtyard is not.
use_when: writing the story and board names of a tactics option
do: Name the grid in the story ("the courtyard tiles")
Guards as sentries or scarecrows
Tables as stalls, haystacks or crates
avoid: Temple courtyards or sacred objects as squares or targets
Themes with no natural grid (open sky, ocean waves)
Real royal palaces

title: Themes that suit a runner route
text: Runner themes need a path that makes sense to walk: a lantern trail, a market street, a parade, a canal bank, a pier, a mountain path, a castle tour, a treasure map. Choose a theme whose checkpoints can be named in a sequence (stall 1 to 5, gate to throne, recipe steps). Lantern trails and markets suit night; parades, piers and farms suit noon; ghost villages suit spooky.
use_when: choosing the theme and route shape of a runner option
do: Pick a theme with a natural order of stops
Match lighting to the theme and venue
Name each checkpoint to tell the theme
avoid: A theme with no path (a single room scene)
Night themes outdoors in daylight
Labels that do not follow the theme

title: Inspired-by is fine, recreating a named IP is not
text: Creators often say "like" a famous game, film or cartoon. Being inspired by a feeling, a genre or a public-domain myth is fine; copying a named game, film, character, logo, level, costume or distinctive look is not. Thai folklore spirits, Greek myth and Himmapan creatures are traditional and free to use, but a specific film's version of them (its costume, scenes or title) is owned. Always ask what the creator loves about the reference and build that feeling in an original world.
use_when: a brief names an existing game, film, cartoon, character or brand
do: Ask what they love about it (speed, cuteness, spookiness)
Use traditional folklore, not a film's version
Invent names for the world and characters
avoid: Character names or look-alikes from films and games
Brand logos on props
A level layout copied from a famous game

title: Make an original twist in three moves
text: To turn a reference into something original: (1) change the who: a different species, age or role (a gecko knight instead of a famous hero), (2) change the where: move it into a Thai or invented setting (a ninja story in a Lanna rice valley), (3) change the why: a new goal (bring the lanterns home, not save the princess). Combining two unrelated themes, such as Himmapan plus space or pirates plus floating market, often gives a fresh world the library still covers.
use_when: the options phase needs a fresh theme or a creator wants "like X but ours"
do: Change at least two of who, where and why
Combine two catalog themes for a fresh mix
Give the twist a one-line pitch
avoid: A reskin with the same characters and names
Combining themes the catalog does not cover
Mixing sacred symbols into a mash-up

title: No real people: celebrities, influencers, politicians or royals
text: Creators sometimes want a famous singer, footballer, YouTuber or politician in their game. Using a real person's face, name or likeness needs their permission and can be defamatory or illegal (and royals are fully off-limits in Thailand). Offer an invented character with a similar vibe (a "rock star cat", a "football robot") and let the creator design it.
use_when: a brief mentions a real celebrity, influencer, politician or the creator's friends by name
do: Offer an invented character with the same vibe
Let the creator pick its name and colours
Keep real names out of prompts and labels
avoid: Real faces or names in key art prompts
Politicians as enemies or jokes
Classmates or teachers as characters
